raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old middle-eastern man presented with dusky discoloration of his skin involving his upper and lower extremities for 4 years. The discoloration involved the dorsal surfaces of his metacarpals and metatarsals, which appeared only upon exposure to cold temperatures, associated with mild discomfort, and disappeared with rewarming initially. Upon presentation, the discoloration was visible at room temperature.
Upon further questioning, he was found to have been diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis since childhood. During his childhood, he had stiffness upon elbow extension, which was more pronounced on the right side than on the left, as well as stiffness upon movement of his knees. In the past, he also complained of morning stiffness lasting for a few minutes as well as stiffness after sitting for prolonged periods of inactivity which improves throughout the day. Additionally, he had mild periodic swelling of finger joints, but not accompanied by pain or redness. At the present presentation, he denied having fever, joint stiffness or redness, pain, and joint swelling. He also denied weight changes, muscle weakness or tenderness, fatigue, hair loss, visual disturbances, eye or mouth dryness, mouth ulcers, numbness/weakness of the lower extremities, and skin rash. His family history was remarkable for juvenile idiopathic arthritis in both his mother and sister. He was started on iron supplementation since childhood and oral prednisone at age 16 to manage his juvenile idiopathic arthritis; otherwise, he took no other medications. Review of systems was negative for any other complaints, and he denied any history of surgical procedures.
On examination, he was sitting comfortably in no apparent distress, with no pallor of the conjunctiva or lymphadenopathy of the head and neck. Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Rheumatologic exam revealed deformations of the interphalangeal joints bilaterally, with fusiform enlargement of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers, associated with reddish discoloration over the joints of the hands bilaterally, with no gross abnormalities of the nails. Examination of the metatarsals revealed mild erythema without other changes. Examination of knees, elbows, and other joints was unremarkable for any redness, swelling, or deformity. Cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. However, capillaroscopic examination was normal.
Upon evaluation, serologic tests including antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were negative. Serum levels of complements (C3 and C4) were normal. Inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were also within normal limits. Subsequent testing for plasma cryoglobulins returned positive, qualitative analysis of which revealed a faint polyclonal pattern. Investigations for potential viral etiologies, including hepatitis B and C and human immunodeficiency virus, were all negative. The total complement level (CH50) was >60 U/mL. Additional tests including serum protein and urine protein electrophoresis did not reveal a monoclonal gammopathy. Serum creatinine remained within normal limits. He was subsequently diagnosed with cryoglobulinemia, and treatment with rituximab was instituted, for which the patient received a cycle every 6 months in addition to methotrexate. He had a dramatic clinical improvement following the first cycle of therapy. He received two cycles of rituximab thus far and is currently in remission with minimal side effects of therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old Middle Eastern man with juvenile idiopathic arthritis presented with a 4-year history of cold-induced dusky discoloration and mild discomfort over the dorsal surfaces of his hands and feet that had recently become persistent at room temperature.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 years, the patient experienced dusky skin discoloration over the dorsal metacarpals and metatarsals initially triggered by cold exposure and relieved by rewarming, which had progressed to persist continuously at room temperature.
subjective.past_medical_history: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) diagnosed in childhood (manifesting with elbow and knee extension stiffness, brief morning stiffness, and intermittent painless finger joint swelling); positive family history of JIA in his mother and sister. No prior surgical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent acral dorsal hand/foot dusky discoloration; negative at presentation for fever, acute joint pain/swelling, weight changes, muscle weakness, fatigue, alopecia, sicca symptoms, oral ulcers, or paresthesias. Home medications: iron supplementation since childhood and oral prednisone started at age 16.

objective.physical_examination: Sitting comfortably in no distress without conjunctival pallor or head/neck lymphadenopathy. Rheumatologic and cutaneous examination revealed bilateral interphalangeal joint deformities with fusiform enlargement of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, reddish-dusky discoloration overlying the dorsal hand/metacarpal joints, and mild erythema over the dorsal metatarsals, with normal nails and unremarkable knee and elbow exams. Nailfold capillaroscopy and cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurological exams were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: ESR, CRP, serum creatinine, C3, C4, and total hemolytic complement (CH50 >60 U/mL) were all normal. ANA, rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP, ANCA, HBV, HCV, and HIV serologies were negative. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis excluded monoclonal gammopathy, whereas plasma cryoglobulin testing returned positive with qualitative analysis demonstrating a polyclonal (Type III) cryoglobulin pattern.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Type III polyclonal cryoglobulinemia associated with longstanding juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) in an HIV-, HBV-, and HCV-negative 26-year-old male, confirmed by positive plasma cryoglobulins with a polyclonal pattern on immunoelectrophoresis and absence of monoclonal gammopathy or viral hepatitis. Initiated on systemic rituximab (every 6 months, 2 cycles completed) in combination with methotrexate, achieving dramatic clinical resolution of acral discoloration and sustained disease remission.
